Testimony of Edward Polewarcryk on
LD 1586, An Act to Amend the School Budget Referendum
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cuttural Affairs

Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on
Education And Cultural Affairs: I am Edward Polewarczyk, from Wiscasset. I am here today to testify In Favor of L.D. 1586 An Act to Amend the School Budget Referendum.

The School Budget process is defined Title 20-A: Education, Part 2: School Organization,
Chapter 103-A: Regional School Units, Subchapter 4: Financing.
The budget process begins with the superintendent creating a proposed budget for the coming school year. It is then presented to the School Committee for review with the opporttmity for each of the Committee members to question the budget items. Eventually, after a number of work sessions, these budget items are approved by a majority of the School Committee.
A Warrant on the Budget Articles is then presented to the public in an open town meeting.
Where each item can be questioned and eventually voted on by the registered voters at that meeting. Generally only the parents and teachers attend this meeting and of course all items are approved and any attempt to understand is discouraged. Most of the voters are tmaware of this process and do not attend the open town meeting. Finally the proposed budget goes to the voters

for validation.
On June 10, 2025, the voters of Wiscasset will go to the polls and be confronted with a 5 page ballot. Many have not seen this information before coming to the polls. They will choose
among the candidates for members of the Select Board, members of the School Committee as

well as other elected positions.
There will be 52 budget items for the voters to approve. They will vary from a little as $1500
to as much as 1.3 million. The voter has the option to approve or reject each item. He knows
what the value is and can decide whether it is reasonable or not. There is very little information provided but at least there is a value. This is followed by a number of questions dealing with

ordinance changes.

Finally we get to the last page of the ballot and read the Question:

"Do you favor approving the Wiscasset School Department budget for the upcoming school

year that was adopted at the latest Wiscasset School Department budget meeting?

YES

NO"

There is no mention of the amount of this item. And yet this is the largest item in the Town's

budget, accounting for approximately 70% of the property tax rate. Many complain to the Town Clerk and the Select Board about there not being an amount. The response is always "We must comply with the statute" . The least we could do is be

transparent and indicate the amount being approved.
I urge the members of the committee to vote Ought to Pass on LDl586 to include the dollar amount applicable to the specific school budget in the School Budget Validation Referendum.
10047282:
Testimony in Support of LD 1586: "An Act to Amend the Regional School Unit Budget Validation Referendum Law"
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and the distinguished members of the Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs, my name is Harris Van Pate, and I serve as policy analyst for Maine Policy Institute. Maine Policy is a free-market think tank, a nonpartisan, non-profit organization that advocates for individual liberty and economic freedom in Maine. Thank you for the opportunity to submit testimony in support of LD 1586, "An Act to Amend the Regional School Unit Budget Validation Referendum Law."
This straightforward yet important bill would enhance transparency and voter empowerment in regional school unit (RSU) budget referenda by requiring that the budget validation question clearly state the total dollar amount of the proposed school budget.
Under current law, voters are often asked to approve school budgets without seeing the specific financial figure directly in the ballot question. Instead, they must rely on separate educational materials or attend budget meetings to understand the full fiscal impact. While civic engagement is crucial, Maine voters deserve to have essential financial information presented at the most critical decision point: the ballot box.
Including the budget's dollar amount in the referendum question promotes several key principles:
 Transparency: Taxpayers are entitled to know precisely how much funding they are being asked to approve. Vague or incomplete referendum language undermines informed consent.
 Accountability: School districts and their leadership will have a stronger incentive to justify their budget proposals when voters can easily assess and weigh the magnitude of spending.
 Public Trust: Making key budgetary figures explicit fosters greater confidence in the process and strengthens the relationship between local government entities and their constituents.
 Alignment with Best Practices: Other states already require financial disclosures or a clear statement of amounts in bond or budget referenda, or are considering adding that requirement.1 2 Maine should similarly ensure that voters are fully informed.
1 https://wasbo.com/images/wasbo/documents/6/handouts/SC2022_OperationalReferenda.pdf 2 https://wisconsinexaminer.com/2025/03/31/proposed-limits-on-school-referendum-requests-stir-debate/

Furthermore, Maine communities face increasing pressure from rising property taxes, largely driven by educational expenditures. Ensuring voters have transparent access to financial figures is critical to protecting families, seniors, and small business owners from unchecked tax burdens. Full disclosure empowers citizens to strike a balance between a strong commitment to public education and fiscal responsibility.
In conclusion, LD 1586 is a commonsense measure that would strengthen democratic participation, increase government transparency, and respect the rights of Maine voters to make fully informed decisions about how their tax dollars are spent. Maine Policy Institute urges the committee to vote Ought to Pass on LD 1586. Thank you for your time and consideration. I am happy to answer any questions you may have.

What is more we will remind the Committee that school board members are elected by voters. If they
d'isagree with their decisions , they can be challenged and voted out. We encourage the Committee to
empower school board members -- not require their thoughtful budgeting to pass through city councils
and the voters.
We oppose LD 1586 because it promises more confusion for voters. Including the total amount of the
school budget in the ballot question fails to provide context to voters. Many will struggle with
understanding the difference between a school budget of $25 million and $250 million. These figures lack context -- many of us cannot picture what $25 million looks like, let alone what that figure
represents for schools and their budgets. We worry including this figure in the budget validation
question could be misleading or confusing to voters.

In addition such a question may undermine educational needs. The dollar figure lacks context that one
can draw from the various budget meetings school boards conduct while working on their budget. A
single dollar figure will not explain the rising cost of special education, a new, innovative program a school board is trying to implement, or any other nuance.
For these reasons, and others, we oppose LD 15 86, An Act to Amend the Regional School Unit Budget Validation Referendum Law and we support LD 1579.

Testimony of Rep. Marygrace Cimino introducing
L.D. 1586, "An Act to Amend the Regional School Unit Budget Validation Referendum Law"
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural A/fairs

April 30, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and honorable members of the Education and Cultural
Affairs Committee:
My name is Representative Marygrace Cimino, and I represent House District 83, comprised of the beautiful towns of Bridgton, Harrison, and Denmark. I am here today to present LD 1586, "An Act to Amend the Regional School Unit Budget Validation Referendum Law".

This bill is, at its core, a simple transparency bill. It does one straightforward thing: it ensures that
when voters are asked to approve a school budget in a budget validation referendum, they are clearly told the actual dollar amount of that budget.
Right now, many voters receive a ballot that asks them to approve the school budget without stating the total amount being proposed. That lack of information undermines the democratic process. When we ask citizens to weigh in on how public funds are spent, we owe them the courtesy--and the responsibility--of giving them the full picture. That includes the bottom-line
number.
This bill doesn't change the process for developing or approving budgets. It doesn't interfere with
local control. It doesn't alter how school boards or budget committees do their work. It simply ensures that when the public is asked to vote on that budget, they see the full amount printed right
on the ballot.
That level of clarity is something we already expect in nearly every other area of public spending.
We disclose bond amounts in referendums. We include mill rates in tax assessments. Why should
school budgets be any different?
LD 1586 supports informed voting. It respects taxpayers. It builds trust between schools and the
communities they serve by providing full and honest information.
Please support this simple but meaningful step toward better transparency in public education finance. Thank you for your time and consideration.

I would be happy to answer any questions.

Marygrace Cimino
State Representative

District 83 Bridgton, Harrison, Denmark

Testimony of the Maine Municipal Association
In Support Of
LD 1586 - An Act to Amend the Regional School Unit Budget Validation Referendum Law
April 30, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy and members of the Education & Cultural Affairs Committee, my name is Rebecca Lambert, and l am providing testimony in support of LD 1586 on behalf
ofthe Maine Municipal Association's (MMA) elected 70-member Legislative Policy Committee (LPC). MMA
is a nonpartisan, nonprofit member service organization and aims to help provide policy solutions that
work for all residents in Maine and the LPC guides the advocacy efforts and establishes positions on bills
of municipal interest.
This change is a critical step toward ensuring transparency, fostering informed voting, and enhancing the democratic process in our municipalities. The public has a right to understand the full financial implications of their votes, and this simple, yet impactful, change will provide voters with the
clarity they need to make informed decisions about the school budgets that directly affect their lives and
communities.
School budgets are complex and multilayered, and school districts must work in partnership with municipalities to ensure public resources are spent wisely and effectively. By providing a clear, bottom-
line amount on how the school budget will impact voters, will foster trust between local government,
school administrators, and the taxpayer base, and shows that the school district is committed to being open and forthright with the public about the costs involved.
Thank you for your time and considering the municipal perspective.

TESTIMONY IN OPPOSITION TO
L.D. 1586
AN ACT TO AMEND THE REGIONAL SCHOOL UNIT BUDGET VALIDATION REFERENDUM LAW
April 30, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Noonan Murphy, and members of the Joint Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs, I am Robbie Feinberg, the Director of Communications and Government Relations of the Maine School Management Association, testifying on behalf of the legislative committees of the Maine School Boards Association and the Maine School Superintendents Association in opposition to L.D. 1586.
This bill requests to place the total amount of the budget on the Budget Validation Referendum question that provides the vote to approve or disapprove of a school administrative unit's budget for the upcoming fiscal year. Both associations see multiple problems with this practice.
First of all, there are logistic and practical issues with this request. The timing of the creation of the ballots (including absentee ballots) is such that it could be problematic to get the budget total onto the ballot in a timely manner. Town clerks are statutorily required to receive ballots early - absentee ballots must be provided the day after a budget meeting.
Currently, these ballots can be created easily, in advance, at any time, where they now only request a Yes or No vote. L.D. 1586 would require these ballots to be updated with the latest budget numbers and printed within just a few hours, placing a larger administrative burden on both school officials and town clerks. We do not want to see clerks, those responsible for preparing these votes, to be challenged in getting voting materials ready for each budget vote, especially when this is a very busy time, often with other local, state, and national election ballots need to be prepared at the same time.
Moreover, we feel this is unnecessary when Maine law already requires the posting of the school budget within each polling location - not only the total budget amount, but also the amounts requested for each Cost Center subtotal. The amount required for the Essential Programs and Services (EPS) portion of the budget is posted, as is the amount above the EPS amount that the school board is requesting to service the programmatic and facility needs of the school district. Many schools even go beyond and provide last year's budget information to allow residents to compare. This budget information is made available to residents of the school community multiple times, through multiple means, so that residents going to the polls to vote on the school district budget should be well-informed as to the total cost of the school budget for the ensuing fiscal year.
With only a single number on the Budget Validation Referendum ballot, without the full budget picture of requests provided on the ballot, residents could be voting on a budget number blind, without any knowledge or supporting information on which to judge their voting decision. Considering the ample information and context that school districts are already required to provide - and the potential administrative challenges this bill presents, our organizations do not think this is a positive change and urge the Committee to vote Ought Not to Pass on L.D. 1586.

Steven W. Bailey
MSBA Executive Director

Eileen E. King
MSSA Executive Director
